title: Fisherman's rib scarf
subtitle: A deep, stretchy rib that mimics brioche worked flat in a single colour.
excerpt: A straight scarf knitted flat in fisherman's rib on 6 mm needles with bulky-weight yarn, finishing at 22 cm wide by 165 cm long. Fisherman's rib knits every knit stitch through the stitch below on the preceding row, building a deep squishy rib that looks identical to brioche on both faces and is noticeably warmer than a standard 2x2 rib.
sourceNotes: Fisherman's rib stitch appears in Weldon's Practical Knitter (1880s-1900s), Internet Archive, under various names including 'knit below rib' and 'patent stitch'. Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938) documents the knit-below technique, citations only.

glossaryTerms.definition: A stitch pattern that knits every knit stitch through the stitch directly below the current stitch on the needle, rather than through the stitch itself. This creates a deep, squishy rib with twice the visual depth of a standard 1x1 rib, and produces a fabric that is nearly identical on both sides.

Insert the right needle into the stitch one row below the first stitch on the left needle, wrap the yarn, and draw through a loop, then drop both the worked stitch and the stitch above it from the left needle together.
A cast-on forming a neat elastic edge by using the tail and working yarn over two fingers simultaneously.

content.text: This is a straight scarf knitted flat in
fisherman's rib

on 6 mm needles with bulky-weight yarn, finishing at 22 cm wide and 165 cm long. Every knit stitch is worked through the stitch one row below on the left needle, drawing up an extra loop that merges with the stitch above it to form a thick, plush rib column. The fabric is fully reversible and noticeably thicker than a standard 2x2 rib in the same yarn.

Flat construction was chosen because fisherman's rib on straight needles has a simple two-row repeat with no stitch count tracking beyond the initial set-up. The finished scarf needs about 380 m (approximately 300 g) of bulky-weight yarn. The deep rib pulls in tightly off the needles and then relaxes slightly when worn; the stated width is the relaxed measurement. The scarf wraps easily once around the neck and stays in place.
What you need

items.name: Bulky-weight wool or wool-blend yarn
items.substitutions: Any bulky-weight yarn. Wool or a wool-blend gives the best loft; acrylic works but the rib may not spring back as firmly.

items.name: 6 mm needles, straight or circular (UK 4 / US 10)
items.qty: 1 pair or 1 circular 60 cm or longer

content.text: Gauge

14 sts x 18 rows = 10 x 10 cm in fisherman's rib on 6 mm needles, unblocked. The fisherman's rib gauge compresses the width because the knit-below action draws the columns in tightly. Measure the swatch unstretched: the fabric springs back to its natural compressed width once off the needle. One stitch per 10 cm off gauge shifts the finished width by about 1.6 cm. Row gauge drift across the full 297 rows of the body changes the finished length by up to 15 cm.
Stitches used
K (knit): right needle from left to right through front of stitch, wrap yarn counterclockwise, draw loop through.
P (purl): right needle from right to left through front of stitch with yarn in front, wrap yarn, draw loop through to back.
K1b (knit one below)

: insert the right needle tip into the centre of the stitch one row below the first stitch on the left needle (the V directly below). Wrap the yarn and draw through a loop. Drop both the stitch on the left needle and the loop above it off the needle together. One stitch remains on the right needle.
Pattern
Cast on
Use the
long-tail cast-on

to place 32 stitches on the needle. The stitch count must be an even number for 1x1 rib: 32 gives 16 pairs. Before beginning, calculate the tail: tail_cm = (needle circumference mm x stitch count) / 10 + 15. For 6 mm needles (circumference approximately 18.8 mm) and 32 stitches: (18.8 x 32) / 10 + 15 = 60.2 + 15 = about 75 cm. Leave a tail of at least 75 cm before the slip knot.
Stitch count check-in: after the cast-on you should have 32 stitches on the needle.
Body
Set-up row (WS): *K1, P1; repeat from * to end. (32 sts) -- This row establishes the rib before the knit-below technique begins.
Row 1 (RS): *K1b, P1; repeat from * to end. (32 sts)
Row 2 (WS): *K1, P1b; repeat from * to end. (32 sts) -- Note: on the WS row the purl-one-below (P1b) is worked purlwise into the stitch one row below.

Alternative simplified WS row: if P1b feels too complex, work Row 2 as *K1, P1; repeat from * to end, and apply the knit-below only on RS rows. The resulting fabric will still have deep rib character, though it will be slightly less even on the purl side.
Repeat rows 1 and 2 until the scarf measures 165 cm from the cast-on edge. At the halfway mark (approximately row 148, around 82 cm), count your stitches.
Stitch count check-in: at row 148 you should have 32 stitches on the needle.
Bind off

Work a stretchy bind-off: K2tog through back loops, slip the resulting stitch back to the left needle, repeat to end. The stretchy bind-off is important for fisherman's rib because a standard bind-off cinches the elastic fabric and produces a bound-off edge that is visibly tighter than the cast-on edge.
Common faults

Knitting into the wrong stitch below. The stitch one row below is the V sitting just under the stitch on the left needle. If you insert the needle into the stitch two rows below, you pull too large a loop and the fabric develops holes. Always count: one row below, not two.

Stitch count rising. When working K1b, both the loop below and the stitch on the needle must drop off together. If only the stitch on the needle drops and the loop remains, you gain a stitch. After each K1b, confirm the stitch above dropped cleanly.

Fabric looking uneven between RS and WS. This is common if K1b is applied only on RS rows and not on WS rows. For a fully symmetrical fisherman's rib, P1b on WS rows. For a slightly simpler version, accept that the two faces will be very similar but not identical.
Finishing

Weave in both tails along the wrong-side edge of the rib column and trim close. Fisherman's rib does not need blocking. If the two ends look slightly different widths, lay the scarf flat, steam lightly from above, and pat gently while warm.
Care
Handwash in cool water with wool wash. Gently support the wet weight. Lay flat to dry. Measure the width while wet and gently ease to the stated dimension if it has grown slightly.
What to try next

Fisherman's rib leads naturally to brioche stitch. The brioche scarf uses a yarn-over combined with a slip stitch instead of the knit-below technique, but produces a very similar lofty rib. The two-colour brioche scarf extends the same principle into alternating colours.
